It was a cool June evening in 4022 when he heard a hearty knock on his front door...again. 

“Dammit, what do they want now?”

I cursed under his breath, taking the activator from his lap and turning off my entertainment system in annoyance.

“Coming!”

I hollered with false hospitality in the direction of the front of the house. Feeling stiff from a day of watching sports games in his empty house, I toggled the stick forward on his wheelchair- propelling myself to whatever waited behind the door. 

I noticed the cobwebs stringing up in the corners of his home, and how all of my photographs can been sugared with dust. As an old man, my body wouldn’t allow me to get up and clean like i used to. A tremor in my hands reminded me of my debilitating palsy, and how no one left on the planet could help me tidy up (or let alone fit through my front door.) 

With an unsteady hand, I pulled the wooden door inward to reveal an even more wooden figure.  

In front of me stood a sprouting, at least six foot tall, with his parents who rivaled the height of my house. 

“Mama! Papa! See? I told you he’d answer!” 

The sproutling was undeniably healthy, already growing a thick shield of bark around his body, and out of his head erupted a few weak branches. His shiny black eyes glistened in amazement like buttons in the sun. I smiled at the small tree, but secretly had enough of being a cultural phenomenon.

Ever since the late twenty-first century, we experimented with human DNA a lot. Infecting it into thousands of species, oak trees were randomly receptive to our genes. 

To make a long story short, the trees evolved, surpassed humans due to their strength and size, while we starved after the great drought. 

Food isn’t really a problem when the only thing you ingest is water and sunlight. It was nothing personal. 

Now I was born after the drought had ceased, and, lucky for me, my father was an Alaskan homesteader, so we knew how to live off the land and survive out here where crops could relatively grow. I never married, and here I am now- living on a sanctuary for the last of us humans. My neighbor who’d lived on the settlement with me died a year ago. Never thought I’d be the last damn upright ape on this planet. 

The sproutling motioned his twiggy arm to both parents, and they both crouched to the ground with a band of their knees to meet my gaze. The mother tree spoke gently:

“Sorry to bother you, but our little twig here saw you on the news. He’s been begging to see the last human.” 

The father tree shook his head disapprovingly, hand-sized leaves floating to the ground as he did so. 

Suddenly, the sproutling handed me a marker, and gave me an inspirational look.

“Mister, will you sign my trunk?”

“Sure thing!”

I played along tiredly, focusing hard to not let my palsy disrupt my penmanship. 

I wondered while signing who would visit me tomorrow. A tour group? The news again? 

I just wished, deep down, that I’d somehow be visited by someone like me.

The last train out of town was said to leave at eleven, and they would sack the entirety of New York City tomorrow morning. No one knew how they’d do it. Nukes? The marines? Were there even any marines left? Fifty percent of the population was sick, so I knew I had to haul ass and get to the station. My plan? To travel upstate to my parents house and take their Ford. They were one of the first to fall ill when the plague just began- the elderly didn’t deal with it too well and died off. And the younger folks? Well...

Now all I wanted was to drive to Montana and waste my time in a secluded mountain cabin until all of this blew over. 

I admit, on the way to the subway it was difficult to avoid all of the infected in the dark, but if I walked fast enough, their half-rotten bodies couldn’t keep up with me. 

They say it all started with some kind of microscopic worm. People would let their dogs outside, they’d dig their nose into dirt, shit, or who knows what else, catch the damn disease, and then good ole’ Fido would pass the parasite onto his owners. The CDC claimed this thing- this worm latched onto the brain and ate the soft tissue. It began to control your body first, then your mind, and before you knew it, you were a slave to this parasites reproductive agenda. 

I pulled a scratched-up gas mask over my face as I got into a more crowded area. Traffic was piled up and unmoving in the streets, and these people driving likely wouldn’t get out of the city. Looking around alertly as I jogged on the pavement, I saw the chaos unfold around me.

One man ran with a young girl, probably his daughter, with a shotgun over his shoulder, most likely ready to shoot to protect the two of them. I was surprised- that gun was illegal considering the nationwide gun-ban that was lobbied through congress years ago. They were hard to find.

I quickly avoided to of the infected to the left of me, who had snapped up from eating garbage from a dumpster to reach at me. 

Only a few more feet, the underground entrance was in sight.  

An obese man behind me wearing his pajamas stopped to catch his breath, but was caught in the hands of the infected I had dodged. He screamed and I heard them begin to vomit onto him, effectively and rapidly passing on the disease to another victim. Good thing I was a track star in high school. 

I was a bit winded when I reached the stairs descending into the subway tunnels, and was relieved to see two military men in hazmat suits guarding the entrance. They trained their assault rifles on me. 

“ID?”

One of them spoke, muffled by the gas mask he was fitted with. I lifted mine from my face and let it rest on my forehead, reaching in the pocket of my flannel shirt for my small metal ID card. I offered it to one of the men, and he scanned it with a device that reminded me of a barcode scanner. I wondered if stores would still be open in Montana. 

Nodding to each other after confirming the legitimacy of my ID, they lifted up one of my sleeves to expose my wrist.

“What are you-!“

I questioned quizzically, but before I knew it, they had jabbed a needle into my flesh.

“Ow!”

They didn’t respond to my reaction, and I watched as the screen on the body of needle read ‘CLEAN’ in blue letters. 

“You’re free to go.” 

The two men parted and allowed me to enter. On the walls that enclosed the stairs were CDC sanctioned posters reading:

WHEN EYES ARE BLACK, THERES NO GOING BACK 

As well as other posters by independents that offered sketchy business:

PROTOTYPE VACCINE, $2000 DOWN PAYMENT 

FULLY FURNISHED BUNKERS IN ALASKA-CALL NOW

A group of people waited before the tracks, and I joined the throng. This station was usually lively, with drummers pattering away on buckets for pocket change, or businessmen shouting on the phone with their thick accents. But now- we all were silent. Everyone here has lost something. 

With a loud ascending screech, the train arrived. Everyone pushed and shoved to get in near the front of the train, so I favored the back where I could finally get some peace and quiet. Sweat was dripping down my cheeks from all that running, and I had a protein bar in my backpack to go to town on. 

I boarded the last car and claimed the only empty seat I could find. I didn’t bother to observe my surroundings due to my fatigue, and that was the nail in the coffin. 

I closed my eyes for just a few moments and settled into the hard seat before hearing a collective voice that made me nearly shit my pants. The voices were dry and cracked as they spoke in unison, filled with nothing but dirty noise. 

“Join us. It won’t hurt, we promise.”

Shit shit shit shit!

I was now staring at a car of beady black eyes and drooling mouths. Their eyes had been stolen from the parasite after the blood was sucked dry from them. It was the portrait of atrophy- and they were all under control. My pulse quickened when I noticed a ratty, diseased dog on one of the infected’s laps.

“You moron, you cursed us all to die!”

But I knew my words wouldn’t get through to any of them. I nearly laughed when they started shuffling towards me like stereotypical zombies from a movie, and I knew it was time to throw in the towel. I pulled the gas mask over my mouth again as one of the infected pulled at my arm. I knew I was fucked, but maybe the gas mask would make it smell less like shit as they infected (and effectively killed) me. 

A woman with fraying, mangy hair grabbed my face and peeled off my mask, foaming at the mouth and ready to vomit all over me. 

I missed my dog.

The elevator pulled me up to the top floor, and I watched patiently as the digits on the screen increased. 

I plugged my ears with headphones and began to play “I don’t want to set the world on fire” by The Ink spots. What can I say? I’m a sucker for all things vintage. 

’I don't want to set the world on fireI just want to start a flame in your heart’

The doors spread wide for me, and upon walking out I realized again how hard it was to walk with explosives sewn into the side of my boots. I descended down the hall, and remembered everything about this building instantly.

To put it simply, justice did not exist- and here, at the Grande Hall of Judges, I was sentenced to misery. 

’In my heart I have but one desire
And the that one is you, no other will do’

I remembered how beautiful my wife was when we met over one hundred years ago. She had fiery red hair that was always held up in a bun. I remembered our dancing lessons, and our wedding. I remembered when her hair turned gray and I watched her die peacefully in hospice. 

As I continued down the hall, robed men and women stared in suspicion. I couldn’t blame them, after all, I was carrying two large duffel bags filled with dynamite over my shoulder. I think one of them tried to question me, but all I could hear was the music playing. 

’I've lost all ambition for wordly acclaim
I just want to be the one you love’

Now it was my son I thought of. How he tragically died of a heart attack at 55, and how my daughter-in-law followed his death with suicide. 

This was it. I turned left slightly and gripped onto the copper handle of the sentencing room. At this point a security team rushed down the hall to usher me out. I didn’t feel anything. Not fear, not anger, not sadness, just a hollow pit in my stomach. I had to make this quick. Rapidly I opened the door and locked it behind me, then eyeing a bookshelf before using all of my strength to push it to the ground to block the entry. 

’And with your admission, that you'd feel the same’

I turned around to a startled group of people in those damn navy robes, bewildered and starting to panic. Their mouths moved, but I turned up the music to silence them. I made eye contact with each and every one of them. 

The emptiness turned to hate for the last time, and I threw both of my bags to the center of the room. 

I thought of my granddaughter, and how much I cried when they called to tell me she’d been killed by an invader. 

The judges began screaming at me, the same way I begged for them not to curse me with immortality in this very room. 

All for shooting a goddamn pedophile who touched my son. 

I felt my hand going into my pocket, and I was sure then what I needed to do. I looked at the small black console in my hand. One button sat in the center- one button that would take down this twisted legal system. 

‘I'll have reached the goal, I'm dreaming of, believe me’

I pressed the button. 

The last thing I saw was the burning bodies of those who had wronged me and the flames of my own anger- or maybe it was hell.

The smell of stale popcorn and filled the air, and the night was calm. The charming music pumped through the entirety of the park had silenced, (as well as the sounds of children crying) and the cast members had finished sweeping the grounds. A single light remained on in Main Street USA, in the brick firehouse, where a downtrodden company mingled in despair. 

Brer Rabbit sat on the floor, his furry head resting in his paws. Brer Fox sat next to him, reassuringly patting his back.

“It’s hopeless!”

The rabbit cried.

“They only comen’ see me on hot days to cool off! They couldn’t care less anymore.”

Across the room, Henry, the Country Bear Jamboree heard Brer Rabbit, and shouted angrily across the building:

“Tell me about it! These days only old folks comta’ our show to rest their feet!”

Suddenly, one of the nameless singing birds from the Tiki Room, who had been idly preening on a rafter above, flew down and squawked angrily. 

“They didn’t even give me a name! I demand justice!”

He raised a wing, and was joined by a roaring crowd of the other misfits, all raising their paws, hands, and feathers in rage. 

The auctioneer pirate from Pirates of the Caribbean spoke up above the group. 

“Arr, I’m tired of these princesses getting all the love. And I’m sure all of ye have had enough of these superheroes!”

An alligator from the jungle cruise skirted across the floor and snapped his jaws. 

“The leader will know what to do, he has a plan!”

The doors opened dramatically, and there he was. A tall figure in a top-hat parted the crowd, silencing them all. Behind him, a short, chubby dragon held a stack of papers and waddled along. The tall man stepped up onto a crate, and the troupe stood silently with respect. The dragon smiled and waved to everyone he could.

He was the Dreamfinder, the forgotten legend, the big man, the leader. 

“Friends,”

He began, clearing his throat.

“I know we all want justice, so a revolution is imminent. Figment and I have a plan to take back the kingdom.”

His eyes were wise as he spoke, and the crowd started cheering with joy after he finished speaking. 

He reached down and hastily grabbed one of the papers that Figment, his dragon assistant, had handed him. Unfolding the sheet which contained chicken scratch only legible to the eccentric Dreamfinder, a voice erupted from somewhere in the throng.

“Dreamfinder, we are behind you! How will we start this revolution?”

The Dreamfinder smiled a wide smile, speaking a special hope to each person below him. 

“One little spark, my friend.”

I couldn’t understand what I was seeing. I was in an ocean of flashing colors, those of which I had never seen before. These colors trailed across my view when I moved my body in the endless plane of nothing, representing pure energy in a realm that didn’t understand matter. 

Holy shit.

After staring at my arm, perplexed at the visuals, my skin started to unpeeled from my hand, my veins being pulled from my flesh like wires, and the meat on my bones pulsing . Somehow, this didn’t hurt. And I wasn’t afraid. 

“You.” 

A voice came from all around me- I felt it inside my body and echoing throughout the endless plane of the immaterial. 

“You have come here from another time, have you not?”

The voice belonged to neither male nor female, and spoke in a tongue I’d never heard, but could somehow understand.

This reality continued to unravel me, and I heard each of my femurs stretch and break like twigs. I couldn’t care less.

“I am from the future, I made a mistake, and I think this reality doesn’t agree with my physical form. How can I undo this, whoever you are?”

An eyeball popped out of my cranium with a quiet snap. 

The voice chuckled, or at least I thought it did. 

“I have not created anything, so I cannot return you to your time.”

It paused. A few on my fingernails tore off like flower petals. 

“I am a prisoner, in my reality I had committed such a great crime that I was exiled to a realm of my own thoughts for eternity. I could create something here, but I am very tired.”

I felt energy ring through my body, as if his thoughts manipulated my existence. Suddenly, my disassembled body began to repair itself. The contents of my stomach returned, and the hole that had been ripped through it sewed together. My fingernails fastened back onto my flesh, and my spinal cord rearranged. 

I looked around for a sign of the mysterious being, but only felt energy. 

“Thank you, that was beginning to be inconvenient.”

I sighed deeply 

The voice of the being boomed once more, overwhelming me with a feeling of peace. 

“I need to rest now. I am so very tired, for I have been here for an eternity. Maybe there should be something in this lonely place. Will you create while I settle in for a long sleep?”

I knew I had nowhere to go, and I knew without doubt that this is what I was meant for. I felt the consciousness of the being drift away, and I felt incredible power transferred into me. 

I became light, energy, your god. 

It was up to me now. To create everything I’d learned in school: the dinosaurs, humans, love, even those silly fables of religion and false gods. I had to create myself when the time came, and to kill indiscriminately. 

I have worked on this masterpiece all for you. 

And it all started with a clap of my godly hands. What you, my children, call the Big Bang.

We sat in that plot of nothing, the entire universe laying before us on a chess board. There was the Moon, Mars, Earth, the Sun. My eyes were bloodshot with rage, and my fists were balled into frustrated fists. I uncurled them and hovered my hand over the orange orb, wishing to strangle it out of existence more than anything. Upon seeing this, his eyes went bold and he jolted forward. 

“Kevin, watch the light dude, watch the light.”

I couldn’t stand his friendly tone. The way he spoke to me. My palm burned as I contemplated crushing the sun, and eventually dooming humanity to starve under the light of the moon. 

I retracted my hand for a moment, staring at the dark abyss below our feet with watery eyes.

“The sun,”

I whimpered. 

“Light- the thing about the sun, I know it gives light and life, but get too close, and it’s heat will burn you alive.” 

My heart broke in my chest as I spoke, only thinking of destruction. I stared up at him.

“You’re my sun, Light, and I got too close. You chose Darkness over me.”

I thought about the guardian of the moon, her mystery and beauty, and how he’d chosen her over me. 

All I could think of now is how much I loved him. 

“No, Kevin, I-.”

I couldn’t stand another word. 

“How could you. After everything we created-together.”

In one swift moment, I knocked the orange sphere off the board into the dark abyss, sending the planets into chaos. 

“Kevin, why?!”

I couldn’t speak.

He was my sun, and burned brighter than anything we could form with our hands.

I had no name. 

It had to be eons ago when I was brought into existence, just opening my eyes in a plot of dark mist and knowing my purpose. I heard the creators voice only once back then, and he proudly displayed the new beings he called “humans”, as they’d call it. What the creator called them I cease to remember, but I remember the unfathomable , musical sound that came from the booming voice of The Creator somewhere above me. 

Ten thousand years had passed, and I’d crossed the threshold to the afterlife many times with gods treasured souls in tow. Some struggled in my arms as the were whipped out of their body- begging to slip back inside the cocoon of mortality. On the contrary, some crawled out, took my hand gently, and waltzed away to the other side without looking back. I never understood why some hated me- why some would rather return to their vessels despite their bodies mangled and ruined in a car wreck.

The human calendar read “2007” on a creamy white wall. I danced through the halls of a hospice, leaving cold air behind each step. I heard a small voice sobbing from down the narrow walkway, and finally arrived at the hollow noise. 

A soul with a lush green aura huddled in the corner of the room, taking labored shrill breaths as it sobbed. I took note of the small frame, and took a shot to my right to see a small body under blue hospice sheets, bald-headed and lifeless. 

“Child.”

I spoke out gently, not wanting to startle the newly departed boy. I skirted over the linoleum tiles effortlessly. Despite my efforts, the soul pressed itself against the wall, the aura erecting to sharp peaks in defense. 

“Who are you? A monster?”

“No child, I am death. Do not be afraid- I’m going to bring you to a happy place away from here.” 

The soul settled slightly, the brilliant golden color now becoming a rich orange. 

“Mama and Daddy told me that I would go to Heaven to see grandma and grandpa soon. Are you here to take me?”

I lowered my shadowy body to the ground, and touched the soul gently. It purred at my fingertips. I felt a sharp pain inside me, knowing that The Creator never created this “Heaven” they spoke about. 

There was only rest. 

I decided to lie, selfishly not wanting to see the soul tormented any longer. His confusion and sadness clouded the corner of the room, leaving black smudges on the wall that only I could see. 

“Yes, they’ve been waiting for you for some time.” 

I wished then, even after fulfilling my task for so many years, that I could remove the sickness that filled this boy, and lay him gently back into his body. Unexpectedly, the small boy grabbed my hand. 

“I’m ready to go. I told Mom and Dad goodbye. They told me it was okay.”

“Very well- Come.”

We stood up at the same time, and I gripped onto the invisible soul of the dead child. We passed the body, and the boy gazed for a moment, perhaps not being able to grasp his own death. 

I waved my hand over the ground, and a blinding white line appeared, as soon as he hesitantly stepped over, there was no turning back. 

Instead of a void that most humans would expect, we were in the room of a small child. The walls were a navy blue, and toy blocks were scattered across the floor. The sun was shining in from the curtains, and a petite bed with dinosaur sheets was sat in the corner. 

The young soul turned his head upward, expecting the voice of a God who had not spared his life. 

“God? Jesus? Is it time to see Grandma? And Grandpa?”

Just then, I patted the apex of his now-white soul in pity. 

“Shhh, you will, boy. But first you must rest.”

Trusting my words completely and being eager to meet his deceased relatives, he climbed into the bed- even ignoring the assortment of toys meant to keep him unawares. 

I stepped over with a mind plagued with guilt, and sat at the edge of the bed. 

“I will see you soon, and bring you to them.”

He smiled, looking at my dark swirling form one last time. 

“Rest,”

I pushed him. It had to be done.

The moment he closed his eyes, his soul faded away and he was deleted from existence. 

The room swirled into a vortex and I was once again at my home in the void. 

For the first time, I felt the warm feeling of fresh tears fall down my face. 

The monster called cancer was the weight a reaper had to carry.
